```{r, include = FALSE}
# The chunks run against the Spark Connect server in SPARK_REMOTE: the
# site's build starts Spark 4.2.1 in a container and sets it.
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>",
  eval = nzchar(Sys.getenv("SPARK_REMOTE"))
)
```

Spark Connect lets a client run Spark SQL on a remote cluster over gRPC,
but every R route to it so far has gone through a JVM or a Python
environment. zuspark speaks the protocol itself, so all you need to query
a Spark Connect endpoint is R packages: connect, run SQL, and bring the
result back as Arrow or as a data frame.

```{r setup}
library(zuspark)
```

## Connect

`spark_connect()` takes an `sc://` connection string, by default the one in
the `SPARK_REMOTE` environment variable. A local Spark Connect server
listens on port 15002; this article runs against one.

```{r}
con <- spark_connect()
con
spark_version(con)
```

Parameters go after a `;`. `token` sends a bearer token and turns TLS on;
any parameter zuspark doesn't recognise is sent as a request header.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
con <- spark_connect("sc://spark.example.com:443/;token=my-token")
```

For Databricks, `spark_connect_databricks()` builds the string and the
header the workspace needs; see the [Databricks
article](databricks.html).

## Run SQL

`spark_sql()` sends a statement. A query comes back as a `zuspark_query`,
which holds the plan but no rows yet; nothing is read until you ask for it.

```{r}
q <- spark_sql(con, "SELECT id, id * 2 AS twice, CAST(id AS STRING) AS s FROM range(5)")
q
```

`spark_schema()` asks the server for the query's types without running
it. They are Spark's types, as Spark names them.

```{r}
spark_schema(q)
```

Commands such as DDL, DML and `SET` run at once, and `spark_sql()` returns
the rows they produce as a data frame.

```{r}
spark_sql(con, "CREATE OR REPLACE TEMPORARY VIEW small AS SELECT * FROM range(3)")
spark_sql(con, "SHOW VIEWS")
```

## Collect the result

`spark_collect()` runs the query and returns one data frame. It runs it
again every time, so the result is always current.

```{r}
spark_collect(q)
```

Values that R can't hold exactly, such as a `BIGINT` beyond 2^53, are an
error by default. `lossy` chooses their exact text or a widened type
instead.

```{r}
big <- spark_sql(con, "SELECT 9007199254740993 AS id")
conditionMessage(tryCatch(spark_collect(big), error = identity))
spark_collect(big, lossy = "character")
spark_collect(big, lossy = "allow")
```

`spark_fetch()` returns the result as an Arrow stream instead, for code
that consumes Arrow directly, and `spark_execute()` runs a statement only
for its effect, returning the number of rows it produced.

```{r}
stream <- spark_fetch(q)
zuarrow::arrow_schema(stream)
n <- spark_execute(con, "SELECT * FROM range(1000000)")
n
```

## Errors

Spark's errors arrive as a `zuspark_sql_error`, with Spark's error class
and SQLSTATE. `spark_error_details()` asks the server for the rest.

```{r}
err <- tryCatch(spark_sql(con, "SELECT * FROM no_such_table"), error = identity)
class(err)
err$error_class
err$sql_state
details <- spark_error_details(err)
names(details[[1]])
head(details[[1]]$stack, 3)
```

## Settings, interrupts and disconnecting

`spark_config()` reads the session's settings, or sets them by name and
returns the values they had. An R interrupt (Ctrl-C, Esc) while a query
runs stops it on the server; `spark_interrupt()` stops every operation of
the session. `spark_disconnect()` releases the session.

```{r}
old <- spark_config(con, spark.sql.session.timeZone = "UTC")
old
spark_config(con, "spark.sql.session.timeZone")
spark_interrupt(con)
spark_disconnect(con)
```
